notes.h: Purpose of the Family Home Protection Act 1976
notes.b: Without this law, a spouse who owned the family home could sell or mortgage it without the other knowing and leave the family homeless. The Act gives the family, and especially the children, security of a home.
points: The family home is the dwelling in which the spouses ordinarily live together as their home. The Act protects the family from losing it because one spouse deals with it alone.
The spouse who does not own the home, and any dependent children, are the people the Act mainly protects, because they are the ones who would lose their home if the owner sold it.
The Act protects the family home whether it is owned outright or held in only one spouse's name, so whose name is on the title deeds (the documents that show ownership) makes no difference.
A spouse with no legal ownership of the home is still protected. The Act does not make that spouse an owner; it gives a veto, meaning the power to block a sale, lease or mortgage of the home.
The protection depends on marriage and applies while the spouses are married and living together in the home. Unmarried cohabiting couples are not covered by this Act.
The Act is in force as amended by the Family Law Act 1995.
notes.tip: If asked how the Act protects the family, give two points: the home cannot be sold, leased or mortgaged without the other spouse's consent, and the consent must be in writing. Add that it applies regardless of who owns the home, and that the family has security of a home.

notes.h: Consent needed to deal with the family home
notes.b: The core of the Act is a consent rule. One spouse cannot deal with the family home alone, and the agreement of the other spouse must be written and given in advance.
points: A spouse cannot sell, lease (let to someone else for a period) or mortgage (borrow money using the home as security) the family home without the written consent of the other spouse. All three actions are covered.
The consent must be given before the deal (prior consent), so agreement given afterwards does not meet the rule.
Consent must be in writing, so an oral agreement to a sale is not enough. A general written consent given in advance can count as consent for later deals, following the 1995 amendment.
If the required consent is missing, the sale, lease or mortgage is void, which means it has no legal effect, and this is why the rule protects the family so strongly.
Under s.3(8)(b), a dealing without consent is treated as not void unless a court declares it void or the parties state in writing within six years that it is void.
There are limited exceptions to the voidness rule, such as a purchaser who paid full value and did not know it was the family home.
A purchaser or lender should check that the required spousal consent has been given before completing a transaction involving the home, because without it the deal may be void.
notes.tip: Examiners reward the three verbs, sell, lease and mortgage, and the word written. Do not write only that a spouse cannot sell without consent, and remember that consent must be prior and written, not oral and not given afterwards.

notes.b: The Act works as a sequence of steps, from checking that the home is covered to what happens if the rules are ignored or consent is refused.
points: 1. Establish that the property is the family home, meaning the dwelling where the spouses ordinarily live together.
2. Before any sale, lease or mortgage, the owner-spouse must obtain the other spouse's written consent.

3. If consent is withheld unreasonably, the owner-spouse can apply to the court to dispense with (do without) the consent. The court does so only where it is unreasonable to withhold it, taking all circumstances into account, including the needs of any dependent children.
4. If a transaction goes ahead without the required consent, it is void, because the Act itself says so, and it has no legal effect.

The court can also dispense with or give the consent where the other spouse cannot be found after reasonable enquiries, lacks the mental capacity to consent, or has deserted, so a missing or incapable spouse does not block every deal.
notes.tip: In the process, the court's role is to dispense with consent where it is unreasonably withheld. A deal made without prior written consent is void by the Act itself, so do not say the non-consenting spouse must ask the court to set it aside.

notes.h: Link to housing finance and to separation and divorce
notes.b: The Act has practical effects on lenders, and it is one of several laws that protect a family when a marriage breaks down.
points: A lender taking a mortgage over a family home will want the other spouse's written consent before it lends, which is the practical effect of the Act on housing finance.
The protection is in addition to any ownership rights, so it does not depend on whose name appears on the title deeds.
The Family Home Protection Act protects the home during the marriage. On judicial separation or divorce, the court can make orders about who keeps the family home as part of its wider powers.

Under the Judicial Separation and Family Law Reform Act 1989 and the Family Law (Divorce) Act 1996, a court can make property orders that transfer or adjust ownership of the family home between the spouses.
notes.tip: In a 12-mark question on how family law protects members when a marriage breaks down, name this Act with one sentence: one spouse cannot sell or remortgage the family home alone. In a question on a couple's rights and responsibilities in marriage, say the home is protected by this Act.

keyTerms.definition: The dwelling in which the spouses ordinarily live together, protected by the Act whoever owns it.
The right of a spouse to live in the family home, which the Act protects even where that spouse does not own it.
Agreement given in writing by one spouse before the other spouse sells, leases or mortgages the family home.
Any transaction that transfers or charges an interest in the family home, such as a sale, lease or mortgage.
A court order allowing a transaction to go ahead without a spouse's consent, in limited circumstances.
An entry registered against a property's title to record a right, such as a spouse's right of occupation, that binds future owners.

factCards.term: Requirement before selling the family home
factCards.definition: The other spouse must give written consent, or the court must dispense with it.

factCards.term: Who can occupy the family home
factCards.definition: A spouse who does not own the home still has a right of occupation that the Act protects.

factCards.term: Status of a transaction made without consent
factCards.definition: It is open to being set aside by the court.

factCards.term: Where the spouse's right of occupation is recorded
factCards.definition: It can be registered as a burden on the title of the property.

questions.prompt: Explain why a spouse who does not own the family home is protected by the Family Home Protection Act 1976.
questions.model: The Act gives a spouse a right of occupation in the family home, the dwelling in which the spouses ordinarily live together, even where that spouse does not hold legal title. A spouse cannot sell, lease or mortgage the home without the written consent of the other spouse. The non-owning spouse can therefore remain in the home and prevent it being dealt with without agreement.

questions.prompt: Outline how the Family Home Protection Act 1976 protects the family home and explain the role of consent in this protection.
questions.model: The family home is the dwelling where the spouses ordinarily live together, and the Act protects it whatever the ownership arrangements. A spouse who has no legal title keeps a right of occupation. Neither spouse may sell, lease or mortgage the home without the other's written consent. Where consent is withheld unreasonably, the court can dispense with it in certain circumstances. A transaction made without the required consent can be set aside by the court. A spouse's right of occupation can be registered as a burden on the title, so future buyers and lenders are on notice. Consent also matters for mortgage finance, since a lender will usually require both spouses to consent to a mortgage over the family home.
